shell.def: The program inside the terminal that reads your commands; on a modern Mac it is zsh. Paths, pipes and environment variables are shell ideas.
levels: The shell is the little helper inside the terminal that listens to what you type and does it. You type 'make a sandwich' in shell-speak and it goes and makes it. It only understands its own special words, so you have to learn its language first.

The shell is the program that runs inside the terminal and reads the commands you type, like `cd` and `ls`, and carries them out. On a Mac the shell is usually zsh, though some computers use bash instead. It can chain commands together, sending the output of one into the input of another, and it remembers settings called environment variables. Typing `echo $SHELL` prints which one you are using.

The shell parses each line you type into a command, its arguments, and any special symbols such as `|` (pipe), `>` (redirect), and `$VAR` (variable expansion), then runs the result. `export PEMS_USERNAME=you` sets an environment variable that child processes inherit; `which python` asks the shell which file on `PATH` will run when you type `python`. Example: `cat 02_collect_events.py | grep def | wc -l` runs three programs and pipes each one's output into the next.

The shell is a full programming language with variables, conditionals, loops and functions, layered under an interactive read-eval-print loop; `.zshrc` configures it at startup, and `.env` files are loaded by scripts rather than by the shell itself. Everything the shell manipulates is text, arguments, output, environment variables, which is powerful and also the source of quoting bugs when a filename has a space in it. It fails silently by default: a failing command in the middle of a pipeline does not stop the ones after it unless you opt in with `set -e` and `pipefail`. Scripts written for interactive use often break when run non-interactively, in cron or a CI job, because aliases and functions from `.zshrc` are not loaded there.

The shell sits at the boundary between the OS's process model, fork and exec, file descriptors, signals, and human convenience, and that boundary explains most of its rough edges: a pipeline is several processes running concurrently connected by kernel pipes, so `set -o pipefail` is required to catch a failure anywhere but the last stage. Practitioners get bitten by unquoted variable expansion, `rm -rf $DIR/*` when `$DIR` is empty can delete far more than intended, by relying on shell aliases inside scripts, which are not expanded non-interactively, and by assuming `cd` in a subshell persists in the parent shell. The tradeoff in a data pipeline is expressiveness versus auditability: a one-line shell pipeline is fast to write and fragile to review, while the same logic in Python is longer but testable. `set -euo pipefail` at the top of every script is the cheapest fix for most of these failure modes.

At production scale the shell mostly recedes into thin glue, a Makefile target, a launchd plist, a CI step, while the real logic moves to a typed language, because shell has no type system and its error handling composes badly across large scripts. What survives is its role as the universal debugging interface: ssh into a machine, and the shell is still there when everything else is broken. An open practical question in ML infrastructure is how much of that surface, piping, redirection, environment inheritance, should move to structured tools like typed task runners without losing the low ceremony that makes the shell fast for one-off investigation.

pip.def: The tool that installs Python libraries: `pip install pandas`. `requirements.txt` lists everything the project needs so `pip install -r requirements.txt` installs it all.
levels: pip is like a delivery truck for your computer. You tell it the name of a toy you want, like 'pandas', and it goes and fetches it and puts it in your toybox. You never have to build the toy yourself.

pip is the command that installs Python libraries, the packages of code other people wrote so you do not have to write it yourself. `pip install pandas` downloads pandas and everything it needs. A `requirements.txt` file lists every package a project needs, one per line, so `pip install -r requirements.txt` installs them all at once.

pip downloads a package from the Python Package Index, resolves its declared dependencies, and installs it into whichever Python environment is currently active. `pip install pandas==2.2.2` pins an exact version; `pip freeze > requirements.txt` writes down every installed package and its version so the environment can be rebuilt. Running pip outside a virtual environment installs into the system Python, which is the mistake `python -m venv .venv` exists to prevent.

pip's job is dependency resolution: given a set of requested packages, find versions that satisfy every package's declared constraints, a hard problem that pip's modern resolver, since 2020, solves by backtracking properly rather than guessing. It installs prebuilt wheels when one matches your platform and Python version, and falls back to building from source when it does not, which is where compiler and BLAS mismatches on Apple silicon show up. `requirements.txt` pins top-level packages but not always their transitive dependencies unless it was generated by `pip freeze`, which is why two 'identical' installs can still drift apart. pip has no environment concept of its own; it always installs into whatever `python` currently resolves to, which is why the venv matters at least as much as pip itself.

The unpinned-transitive-dependency problem is real: a `requirements.txt` with only top-level packages can resolve to different versions months apart as upstream packages release, silently changing numerical results, which is why reproducible pipelines use a lock file, pip-tools, uv, or conda-lock, that pins every package in the graph, direct and transitive. Practitioners get bitten by mixing pip and conda in the same environment, which can corrupt binary compatibility for packages like numpy that ship compiled extensions. The tradeoff pip embodies is speed and simplicity of the tool versus correctness of the result: it will happily install a set of versions that satisfy the stated constraints but conflict at runtime in ways it cannot detect, because Python has no strict ABI enforcement across packages.

At scale, teams stop calling pip directly and instead build and publish internal wheels through an artifact repository, so a training job's dependency set is fixed at build time rather than resolved fresh on every machine, removing pip's resolution step from the hot path entirely. Reproducibility audits increasingly require a full lock file plus a hash of each wheel, since a supply-chain compromise of a single transitive dependency on PyPI is a realistic attack surface. The open tooling question is whether Python's ecosystem converges on one fast, correct resolver, uv is the current leading contender, the way other languages did with Cargo or npm, since pip's resolver, while now correct, remains slow on large dependency graphs.

csv.def: Comma-separated values: a text table, one row per line, commas between fields. Easy to read, slow and large.
levels: A CSV is like a shopping list written on lined paper, one item per line, with commas splitting the name from the price. Anyone can open it and read it, even without a fancy program.

A CSV file stores a table as plain text: each line is a row, and commas separate the columns within that row. You can open one in a text editor, in Excel, or read it into Python with `pandas.read_csv`. A PeMS detector file might have columns for the time, the station number, and the speed, all comma-separated on one line per five-minute reading.

A CSV has no built-in types: every value is text until something parses it, so a date column reads in as a string and must be converted with `pd.to_datetime`. `pd.read_csv('file.csv', header=None, names=[...])` reads a file with no header row and assigns column names explicitly, which the PeMS files require. CSV also has no schema enforcement, so a stray comma inside an unquoted field, or a column that is sometimes an integer and sometimes empty, can silently corrupt the table unless it is checked.

CSV's assumptions are minimal by design, no types, no compression, no indexing, which makes it universally readable but expensive: parsing text into typed values takes real CPU time, and a month of five-minute detector rows across hundreds of stations can be hundreds of megabytes as text versus a fraction of that as compressed columnar Parquet. It fails on data with commas or newlines inside a field unless the writer quotes correctly, and different tools disagree at the edges, quoting, encoding, line endings, which is the source of most 'my CSV won't parse' bugs. `pd.read_csv` accepts a gzipped file directly and infers most of this, but explicit `dtype` and `parse_dates` arguments make loading both faster and less error-prone than letting pandas guess.

CSV is text, so it stores no data type, no null-versus-empty-string distinction beyond convention, and no per-column encoding, which pushes correctness work downstream into every reader's parsing code; a known failure mode is a numeric ID like a station code getting silently reinterpreted, dropping a leading zero, when a spreadsheet program round-trips the file. At scale, row-oriented text has poor compression and forces reading whole rows even when only one column is needed, which is exactly what columnar formats fix; the tradeoff practitioners weigh is CSV's universal compatibility against Parquet's speed, size and type safety for anything beyond a one-off inspection. A common mistake is treating a CSV export as a stable interface when the producing system silently changes column order or adds a column, which breaks a `names=[...]` argument written for the old schema.

In production data platforms, CSV survives mainly as an ingestion and interchange format at the edges, the format a third-party vendor or public agency like PeMS actually ships, while everything internal moves to columnar formats within minutes of arrival, precisely because CSV's lack of schema makes it unsafe to depend on directly at scale. Schema-on-read tooling and data-quality frameworks exist largely to catch the failure modes CSV allows silently. The frontier problem is less about the format itself than about provenance: knowing, for every row in a warehouse, which CSV export it came from and whether that export's schema changed underneath you.

polling.def: Asking a server for its current data on a schedule, as the 511 collector does every few minutes.
levels: Polling is like asking 'are we there yet?' over and over on a car trip. Every few minutes you ask again, and most of the time the answer is the same as last time. Eventually the answer changes and you find out.

Polling means a program repeatedly asks a server for its current data instead of waiting to be told. The 511 traffic collector polls the 511.org API every few minutes, asking what events are active right now, and saves whatever comes back. If nothing changed since the last check, the program just asks again later.

A polling loop runs on a fixed interval, `time.sleep(interval)` between requests, and each call is a fresh request-response cycle over HTTP, unlike a persistent connection. `requests.get(url, params={'api_key': KEY})` followed by `.json()` is one poll; wrapping it in a loop with `try/except` around the network call handles the request that inevitably fails. Polling too often wastes requests and can hit a rate limit; polling too rarely means missing short-lived events, so the interval is chosen to match how fast the underlying data actually changes.

Polling trades efficiency for simplicity: it is stateless and easy to reason about, but it wastes bandwidth and server load on unchanged data, and its update latency is bounded below by the polling interval, so an event lasting less time than that interval can be missed entirely. It assumes the server has no cheaper way to notify you; the alternative, a webhook or a streaming subscription, pushes changes as they happen but requires the server to support it and requires you to run something that can receive pushes. `asyncio` lets one process poll several endpoints concurrently with a shared rate limiter, which matters once a collector watches many data sources rather than one. Failures are transient by nature, a timeout, a 500, so a robust poller retries with backoff rather than crashing on the first bad response.

The theoretical tradeoff is the same one behind cache invalidation and eventual consistency: polling interval versus staleness versus load, and no interval is simultaneously cheap, fresh and safe against rate limits, so production systems adapt the interval, polling faster right after a change, backing off when nothing changes, or move to a hybrid where a cheap check for a version number gates a full fetch. A subtle bug practitioners hit is assuming polls are safe to overlap; if a poll takes longer than the interval, overlapping requests can arrive out of order and a naive 'last write wins' save can silently revert to older data. Clock skew and the API's own server-side caching mean polling faster than that cache's TTL buys nothing but looks like it is working.

At scale, polling many external sources becomes its own infrastructure problem, a scheduler that respects per-source rate limits, deduplicates near-identical responses, and emits a clean event stream downstream regardless of how each source actually exposes its data, because the rest of the pipeline should not care whether the upstream was polled or pushed. The open tension is between the operational simplicity of polling, nothing to expose, easy to debug, works behind any firewall, and the freshness and cost advantages of push-based ingestion, and most production traffic and events pipelines end up running both, polling as the reliable fallback under a push path that occasionally drops messages.

flow.def: Vehicles counted passing the detector in the interval.
levels: Flow is how many cars zoom past a spot on the road while you count for five minutes, like counting sheep jumping a fence.

Flow is the number of vehicles a detector counts passing over it during one measurement interval, usually five minutes on PeMS. A station reporting a flow of 400 means 400 vehicles crossed that point on the freeway in those five minutes. High flow with high speed means traffic is moving well; high flow with low speed can be the start of congestion.

Flow is measured in vehicles per interval, often scaled to vehicles per hour, alongside occupancy, the share of time a vehicle sat over the sensor, and speed, which together describe traffic at one point on the road. `df.flow` in the PeMS-processed table is one such column; speed is sometimes estimated from flow and occupancy with an assumed vehicle length rather than measured directly. Flow alone is ambiguous: a flow of zero can mean an empty road or a gridlocked one, which is why it is read together with speed.

Flow is the dependent variable of the fundamental diagram: as density rises from empty, flow rises roughly linearly until the road nears capacity, then falls as vehicles pack in and everyone slows, so the same flow value can correspond to two very different traffic states, one free-flowing and one congested, distinguished only by speed. It is measured by loop detectors counting axle-pair pulses, which fails or double-counts under specific failure modes, a stuck-on loop reports occupancy near 100 percent and flow near zero even in free traffic. Flow features in this project appear mainly as lags and rolling means alongside speed, since flow's fundamental-diagram relationship to speed carries information a speed-only model misses, particularly right at the onset of a breakdown.

Flow is a count, not a rate, so its variance scales with its mean in a way closer to Poisson than Gaussian, which matters if you model it directly, a Poisson GLM on flow counts gets the calibration of predicted variance right in a way squared-error regression does not, even though this project mostly consumes flow as a feature rather than a target. A subtlety practitioners miss: flow drops during an incident not because fewer cars want to travel but because the road's capacity has fallen, so a falling flow reading downstream of a detector can itself be an early signal of the exact breakdown the model is trying to predict, distinct from and complementary to a falling speed reading. Detector calibration, the assumed vehicle length used to convert occupancy and flow into a speed estimate, drifts over years and differs by lane, a source of slow, hard-to-detect bias in flow-derived features across a sensor network.

Production traffic systems fuse flow from heterogeneous sensors, inductive loops, radar, and increasingly probe-vehicle GPS traces that report speed but no true flow at all, so flow as a first-class signal is being partly displaced by probe-derived features that skip counting vehicles entirely. Open research questions include how to fill in flow for probe-only corridors via network-flow conservation constraints across a graph of intersections, and how to make flow-based features robust to the loop-detector failure modes, stuck sensors, miscounts under congestion, that are common enough in any real deployment to need explicit anomaly detection rather than trust.

nan.def: Not a number / not a time: the markers for a missing value. Most pandas functions skip them; `fillna` replaces them.
levels: NaN is the computer's way of shrugging and saying 'I don't know that number.' Instead of leaving a blank hole, it writes a special word so you can tell something is missing on purpose.

NaN, not a number, and NaT, not a time, are special markers pandas uses for a missing value in a numeric or a datetime column. If a detector was offline for one reading, that row's speed becomes NaN instead of zero, because zero would falsely mean the road was empty. Most pandas functions like `.mean()` skip NaN automatically; `fillna(0)` replaces it with a chosen value when you want to.

`np.nan` is a special floating-point value defined by the IEEE 754 standard, and it is contagious: any arithmetic involving it produces NaN, and `NaN == NaN` is `False`, so you must test with `pd.isna(x)` rather than equality. `df.speed.shift(3)` creates NaN in the first three rows because there is no data above them to shift down. `df.dropna(subset=['y_15','y_30','y_60'])` removes rows where any of the three label columns is NaN, which is exactly the rows near the end of each month with no future to look into.

NaN represents 'missing' but conflates several distinct causes, a sensor outage, a value outside a plausible range that was masked out, a lag with nothing above it, a target with nothing below it, and treating all of these the same is an assumption that can bias a model if the causes are not missing at random. Integer columns cannot hold NaN in older numpy or pandas without being upcast to float, which is why a count column can silently change dtype; nullable integer types fix this. Most scikit-learn estimators cannot handle NaN at all and will throw at fit time, while LightGBM handles it natively by learning a default split direction for missing values, one reason gradient-boosted trees are convenient on real sensor data.

The right handling of NaN depends on the missingness mechanism, MCAR, MAR or MNAR in Rubin's taxonomy: a detector failing under congestion is missing not at random, correlated with exactly the event being predicted, so dropping those rows or imputing them with a typical value biases the label distribution in a predictable direction. Practitioners commonly get this wrong by imputing with a column mean before splitting into train and validation, leaking information across the split, and by silently converting NaN to a sentinel like -1 that a tree model then treats as a real, extreme value rather than as missing, distorting splits. The tradeoff between dropping NaN rows and imputing has no universally correct answer and should be checked empirically per feature.

Production feature pipelines at scale make missingness itself a feature: a boolean 'was this station reporting' column often carries real predictive signal beyond the imputed value, because sensor failure correlates with the events being predicted. Systems increasingly formalize missing-data handling in the feature store itself, versioned imputation logic, so a change to how NaN is handled is auditable and reproducible rather than scattered across notebooks. An open engineering problem is propagating missingness provenance through a deep pipeline of joins and aggregations so that by the time a value reaches a model, you can still answer whether a NaN meant no sensor or a filtered implausible reading.

array.def: A grid of numbers: one-dimensional (vector), two-dimensional (matrix), or more. PyTorch calls its arrays tensors.
levels: An array is a row of number boxes lined up like an egg carton. A matrix is a grid of them, like a chessboard of numbers. A tensor is what grown-ups call it once the grid has more dimensions than you can draw.

A one-dimensional array, also called a vector, is a list of numbers, like the speeds at one station over an hour. A two-dimensional array, a matrix, is a table of numbers with rows and columns, like every station's speed at every five-minute slot. In PyTorch, arrays of any number of dimensions are called tensors, and `torch.tensor([1,2,3])` makes one.

NumPy stores an array's numbers as one flat block of memory plus a shape describing how to read it as rows and columns, which is why operations like `np.exp(arr)` run fast, they act on the whole block at once instead of looping in Python. `X.shape` for a feature table might be `(50000, 20)`, 50000 rows, 20 columns. A PyTorch tensor adds two things an array doesn't have by default: it can live on a GPU, and it can track gradients for backpropagation.

The core assumption behind array-based computing is that most numerical work is naturally expressed as elementwise or broadcasted operations over whole arrays rather than explicit loops, and the underlying implementation exploits that to avoid Python's per-element overhead, often a hundredfold speedup. Broadcasting rules, aligning shapes from the right, stretching size-1 dimensions, let arrays of shapes like `(1000, 5)` and `(5,)` combine without an explicit loop, but silently produce wrong results when shapes accidentally broadcast in an unintended way rather than raising an error. A matrix multiply, `@`, versus an elementwise multiply, `*`, is a common source of shape-mismatch bugs for anyone moving from scalar to array thinking. Tensors extend this to GPUs by mapping the same elementwise and matrix operations onto thousands of parallel cores.

Memory layout, row-major versus column-major order, determines which axis is contiguous in memory, and operations that traverse the non-contiguous axis are slower than they look, a subtlety that shows up in profiling but rarely in tutorials. Practitioners get bitten by implicit dtype upcasting, mixing int32 and float64 silently promotes everything to float64, doubling memory, and by views versus copies, a sliced array can share memory with the original, so mutating it mutates the original unexpectedly. The tradeoff tensors add over plain arrays, autograd bookkeeping and device placement, costs memory and adds a class of bugs, a tensor accidentally left on CPU when the model is on GPU, that arrays never had.

At production scale, array and tensor computation is inseparable from hardware: compilers like XLA and MLIR fuse chains of elementwise and matrix operations into single kernels tuned for the target accelerator, GPU, TPU, or a neural engine, because the naive sequence of separate calls each round-trips through memory and leaves most of the hardware's throughput unused. Quantization, storing a tensor's values in int8 or lower instead of float32, trades numerical precision for memory bandwidth and is now standard for on-device inference. Open research continues on sparse and structured tensor representations that skip storing and computing over the often-majority of near-zero values in large models, since dense array assumptions increasingly overstate the compute actually needed.

shift.def: Move a column down by k rows (a lag). A negative k moves it up, which looks into the future: allowed only for targets.
levels: Shift is like everyone in a line taking one step back and leaving an empty spot at the front. The number tells you how many steps to take.

`shift(k)` moves every value in a column down by k rows, leaving the first k rows empty, NaN, because nothing was above them to move into their place. `df.speed.shift(3)` creates a column showing what the speed was three rows earlier, exactly a lag feature: what the model knew fifteen minutes ago on a five-minute grid.

`df['speed_lag_3'] = df.speed.shift(3)` shifts values down by 3 rows; the value that used to sit at row 100 now sits at row 103, and rows 0 through 2 become NaN because there is nothing above them. A negative argument shifts up instead: `df.shift(-6)` moves row 106's value up to row 100, looking six rows into the future, so it is used only to build the target column, never a feature, or the model would train on information it cannot have at prediction time. `df.groupby('station_id').speed.shift(3)` shifts within each station separately so a lag never crosses from one station's data into another's.

A positive shift is always safe to use as a feature because it only reaches into the past, while a negative shift reaches into the future and defines the label the model is trying to predict, so mixing the two up, accidentally training on a negative-shifted column as a feature, is the single most common way to leak the answer into the inputs. Shift assumes rows are already sorted by time within each group; an unsorted DataFrame produces a shift that is nonsense but doesn't error, a silent-failure risk. At the boundaries of the data, start and end of each month's file, or a gap where a station went offline, shift produces NaN rows that must be dropped before training rather than imputed, since there is no honest value for 'the reading fifteen minutes ago' when fifteen minutes ago doesn't exist in the file.

`shift` is the atomic operation behind almost every classical time-series feature, lags, rolling statistics, differences, and its main pitfall in practice is scope: shifting on a DataFrame sorted globally by time but not grouped by station silently pulls in another station's last reading as this station's lag, a bug that will not raise an error and will look like real signal in a naive train and validation split, since it inflates apparent accuracy through a form of leakage. A related subtlety: at inference time in a streaming setting, `shift(3)` on a static DataFrame and 'the reading three steps ago from a growing buffer' are the same operation conceptually, but implementing the second one correctly, right buffer size, no off-by-one at the boundary, is where most production time-series bugs actually live, not in the training-time pandas code.

In production feature pipelines, `shift`-based lag computation moves from a single-machine pandas call to a window function in a distributed engine, `LAG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY station_id ORDER BY ts)` in SQL, or a streaming state store keyed by station, and the two must be proven to produce identical results, a routine and easy-to-get-wrong reconciliation between offline training features and online serving features. Feature stores increasingly compute and cache these lag features once, shared across many models, rather than recomputing per model, since the same handful of lags, 3, 6, 12 steps, tend to recur across a whole traffic-prediction product line.

assert.def: A check that must be true or the program stops with an error. The cheapest safety net; put one before every write.
levels: assert is like a grown-up double-checking your shoes are tied before you run outside. If they aren't, everything stops right there instead of letting you trip later.

`assert` checks that something is true, and if it isn't, the program stops immediately with an error message instead of continuing with bad data. `assert df.speed.between(0, 100).all()` stops the program if any speed value is outside a sane range. It is the cheapest safety net in the whole toolkit, one line, no library needed.

`assert condition, 'message'` raises an `AssertionError` with that message if `condition` is falsy, and does nothing at all if it is true. `assert not df.duplicated(['station_id','timestamp']).any(), 'duplicate rows found'` is a good check to run right after loading raw data and right before writing processed data, since it catches a whole class of silent corruption. Python can strip out all asserts when run with `python -O`, which is why asserts should check invariants that are cheap to verify, not substitute for real input validation on untrusted data.

The convention this course follows, an assert before every write, treats data pipelines the way software engineering treats unit tests: cheap, local checks that fail loudly and immediately rather than letting a bad value propagate silently three stages downstream where it is much harder to trace back. Assertions check invariants the programmer believes must hold, row counts match after a join, no NaN in a column that should be complete, a probability stays within 0 and 1, which is different from `try/except`, which handles conditions the programmer expects might legitimately happen, like a network timeout. The `-O` flag stripping asserts means code that depends on side effects inside an assert statement, a rare but real bug pattern, breaks silently in optimized mode.

There is a real design tension between asserting broadly, catches more bugs but can make a pipeline brittle, halting a nightly job over a borderline case a human would have shrugged off, and asserting narrowly, which misses real corruption. Practitioners often get the granularity wrong in both directions: too few asserts, and a labeling bug from an earlier stage ships silently into a model that trains and evaluates 'fine' because nothing crashed; too many rigid asserts, and a legitimate seasonal shift trips an alarm that should have been a warning, not a halt. A more mature pattern at scale is a data-quality framework that runs the same checks as configuration rather than code, distinguishing hard failures from soft warnings and logging both.

In production ML systems, the descendants of a scattered `assert` statement are schema validation at ingestion, data contracts between teams that produce and consume a dataset, and automated data-quality monitoring that runs the equivalent of hundreds of assertions continuously and alerts rather than crashing a running service. The open problem is less whether to assert and more how to keep the set of assertions in sync with an evolving pipeline, stale assertions that no longer reflect the data's real invariants are a common source of alert fatigue, and some teams now generate expected-range assertions automatically from historical data rather than hand-writing every threshold.

profile.def: The typical speed per station, day type and slot, computed as the median over training rows only.
levels: The profile is what's normal for a road at a certain time, like knowing your friend is usually happy in the morning, so you can tell when something's off.

The profile is the typical speed at a station for a given day type, weekday or weekend, and time slot, computed as the median speed over the training data only. It is the 'normal' the model compares each new reading against: 40 mph might be perfectly normal at 2 a.m. but slow for 8 a.m. rush hour, and the profile is what lets the model tell the difference.

The profile is built with `train.groupby(['station_id','daytype','slot']).speed.median()`, computing one typical speed per station, per weekday-or-weekend, per five-minute slot of the day, using only the training rows so no information from validation or test leaks in. A cell with too few samples, fewer than about 20 training days, falls back to a coarser aggregation rather than trusting a noisy median. The label is then defined relative to this profile, speed dropping to some ratio below it, rather than against one fixed threshold for every station.

Using a relative profile rather than an absolute speed threshold is a deliberate modeling choice: a freeway station with a free-flow speed of 65 behaves very differently from an on-ramp with a free-flow speed of 40, and an absolute threshold would call the ramp slow constantly. The assumption underneath the profile is that a station's own typical speed by day-type and slot is a stable, meaningful baseline, which holds well in the medium term but degrades slowly as roadwork, seasonal patterns or detector replacement shift what typical actually means. The median, rather than the mean, is used specifically for robustness: a handful of incident days should not drag the profile down and make ordinary slow traffic look extra slow by comparison.

Because the label is defined relative to an estimator, the profile, rather than a fixed rule, label noise inherits the profile estimator's own error, and that error's structure changes with the split: computing the profile on training data only and comparing test rows against it means the test-period positive rate is not pinned at a fixed value by construction, which is correct, but if the profile were instead computed on the test period too, the positive rate would be artificially pinned near a fixed quantile, hiding any real change in typical traffic. A subtlety practitioners get wrong: the median's standard error scales like σ divided by the square root of n, so with roughly forty weekday samples per station-slot cell, smoothing across neighboring time slots trades a little bias for a real reduction in profile noise, and skipping that smoothing makes the label noisier than the underlying traffic actually is.

In production, a profile like this must be versioned and monitored as a first-class artifact, not recomputed ad hoc, because the model's label definition, and therefore its entire meaning, depends on it; retraining with a silently different profile changes what 'slow' means without changing any code that looks like a bug. Open questions include how to update the profile online as roadwork and seasonal patterns shift without either lagging real change or overfitting to recent noise, and whether a smoothed, hierarchical estimate, borrowing strength across nearby stations, not just nearby time slots, improves on the simple per-station median used here.

metric.def: How guesses are scored. Average precision, precision, recall, Brier score, lead time and false-alarm rate are the course's metrics.
levels: A metric is the number that tells you how good a guess was, like counting how many stars you get for cleaning your room.

A metric is a rule for turning a model's predictions into one number that says how good they were. This course uses several: average precision, how well the model ranks likely-slow moments above others, precision and recall, the Brier score, how close predicted probabilities are to the truth, lead time, how early an alert fires, and the false-alarm rate.

Average precision is the area under the precision-recall curve, computed with `sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score(y_true, y_score)`; because only a few percent of rows are truly slow, accuracy is a useless metric here, a model that always predicts not-slow is right most of the time, and average precision, which focuses on ranking true positives near the top, is the right one. The Brier score, the mean of (p - y) squared, checks calibration, whether a predicted 0.3 really corresponds to a 30 percent chance. Lead time and false-alarm rate are computed per episode rather than per row, since what matters operationally is how early and how reliably an alert fires, not the score on any single five-minute slot.

The right metric follows from the decision the model supports, not from convention: because positives are rare, a threshold-free ranking metric like average precision is preferred during development, while a threshold-dependent metric like precision at a fixed recall matters once a specific alerting threshold is chosen for deployment. Average precision assumes the ranking, not the raw probability value, is what's being evaluated, so a model can have excellent average precision and terrible calibration at the same time, exactly why the Brier score and a reliability diagram are reported separately. A model's metric can look great on random validation rows and still fail operationally if episode-level metrics tell a different story, because a per-row metric treats every five-minute slot inside one long slowdown as an independent success, double-counting.

Metrics interact with the label's own definition in ways practitioners commonly miss: because the label is relative to an estimated profile, and prevalence drifts across seasons and roadwork, a single held-out test window is one draw from a moving distribution, so one number is not a reliable comparison between two models, rolling-origin evaluation across multiple folds is needed to see whether an apparent improvement is real or noise. There is a real tradeoff between metrics optimized for ranking and metrics that reward calibrated, decision-useful probabilities, and optimizing purely for the first can produce a model that ranks well but whose raw probabilities are unusable for setting a principled alert threshold. A subtle failure: reporting a metric only in aggregate across all stations hides that a model can be excellent on high-traffic stations and near-useless on low-traffic ones, since the aggregate is dominated by the stations with the most rows.

Production systems typically track a portfolio of metrics rather than one, an offline ranking metric for model comparison, a live calibration check against delayed ground truth for monitoring, and business metrics that the offline metrics are only a proxy for, because no single number captures everything a deployed model needs to get right, and optimizing tightly against just one invites Goodhart's law. An open and genuinely unresolved problem across the industry is metric drift under a moving population: as a model's own alerts change driver behavior, an alerted driver takes a different route, the very traffic pattern the metric is evaluated against changes, breaking the usual assumption that evaluation data reflects the world the model will act in.

drift.def: The data slowly changing after training. Measured with the population stability index; confirmed by delayed scoring.
levels: Drift is when the world slowly changes without telling you, like your shoes fitting fine in September and feeling tight by spring because your feet grew.

Drift is when the data a model sees in production slowly stops looking like the data it was trained on. New roadwork changes typical speeds at a station, a detector gets replaced and reports slightly differently, or driving patterns shift over the seasons, and the model's assumptions quietly become out of date. Drift is measured with the population stability index, comparing a feature's distribution now against its distribution at training time, and confirmed by checking the model's actual accuracy once true outcomes catch up.

The population stability index buckets a feature into bins, compares the share of current data in each bin against the share at training time, and sums a weighted log-ratio across bins; a value above roughly 0.2 is a common rule-of-thumb threshold for meaningful drift. Lag features like `speed_lag_3` are stationary by construction, since they are differences and ratios relative to recent history, while calendar and static features, like a station's typical top speed, drift as roadwork or detector replacement changes what free flow actually looks like there. The index flags a distributional change immediately; confirming it actually hurt the model requires waiting for delayed scoring, matching predictions against ground truth once it arrives.

Drift comes in two flavors that call for different responses: covariate drift, where the input distribution shifts but the relationship between inputs and the label stays the same, and concept drift, where the relationship itself changes, the more dangerous case because retraining on more of the same kind of data does not fix it. The population stability index detects that something changed but not which kind, so it is a trigger for investigation, not a diagnosis. A model can show zero drift on every monitored feature and still be silently wrong if the world changed along a dimension nobody thought to monitor, which is why drift monitoring is complementary to, never a replacement for, tracking real accuracy against delayed ground truth.

A specific subtlety here: lag and rolling-window features are stationary by construction, so a stability index on them will look deceptively calm even while the calendar and static features paired with them are drifting hard, and a monitoring system that only checks the stable-looking features misses the real signal. Practitioners commonly set a drift threshold once and never revisit it, even though the right sensitivity depends on how costly a missed drift event is versus how costly a false alarm that triggers an unnecessary retrain is, the same cost-asymmetry reasoning used to pick the model's own alert threshold, one level up. Retraining blindly in response to detected drift, without checking whether it is concept drift, in which case more historical data does not help, or a genuine permanent shift versus a temporary anomaly, can make a model worse, not better.

In production ML at scale, drift detection runs continuously across thousands of features for many models, and the practical problem shifts from detecting drift, solved, to deciding which of the daily drift alerts deserve a human's attention, since these statistics fire constantly on any system with real-world variability, mostly on features that don't actually matter for the label. Automated retraining pipelines increasingly gate on drift signals combined with a live calibration check, retraining only when both a distributional shift and an actual accuracy drop are observed together, which reduces false-alarm retrains but adds the latency of waiting for ground truth. An open research question is causal drift attribution: given a drifted metric, automatically identifying which upstream feature or data-source change caused it, rather than a human tracing it by hand across a large feature pipeline.

cross-entropy.def: −log p for a true positive, −log(1 − p) for a true negative, averaged. Punishes confident wrong answers heavily.
levels: Cross-entropy is a scorekeeper that gets really mad if you say 'definitely yes' and you were wrong, but only a little mad if you say 'maybe.'

Cross-entropy measures how bad a set of probability predictions is compared to the true answers. For a row that was truly positive, the penalty is minus the log of p, the predicted probability of positive; for a row that was truly negative, it's minus the log of (1 minus p). The model's loss is the average of this penalty over every row, and training tries to make that average as small as possible.

For a binary label y (0 or 1) and predicted probability p, the per-row cross-entropy loss is L = −[y·log(p) + (1−y)·log(1−p)], and the training objective is the average of L over all rows. This is the `objective='binary'` in LightGBM and the loss function logistic regression minimizes. Its shape is what makes it useful: predicting p=0.99 for a row that turns out negative costs far more than predicting p=0.6 for the same mistake, because −log(1−p) grows without bound as p approaches 1.

Cross-entropy loss is derived from maximum likelihood: assuming each label is a Bernoulli draw with probability p, the negative log-likelihood of the observed labels is exactly the cross-entropy sum, so minimizing it is equivalent to maximum-likelihood estimation, not an arbitrary choice of penalty. Its gradient with respect to the raw score z, before the sigmoid, is remarkably clean, ∂L/∂z = p − y, error times nothing else, because the sigmoid's own derivative and the log's derivative cancel in the chain rule, the term at the heart of logistic regression and every neural classifier's output layer. Cross-entropy assumes the labels are correctly specified probabilities of a real event; if the label itself is noisy, as a profile-derived slow label is, the model is technically fitting a noisy likelihood, biasing fitted probabilities toward the label noise's own structure.

Cross-entropy is a proper scoring rule, meaning a model is never better off reporting a probability other than its true belief, exactly why it is the right loss when calibrated probabilities, not just correct rankings, are the goal, unlike hinge loss, which lacks this property. A common mistake is optimizing cross-entropy while separately optimizing a decision threshold on a ranking metric like average precision without checking that the two agree; on imbalanced data they often diverge because cross-entropy's average is dominated by the many easy negatives. Label smoothing, softening y from exactly 0 or 1 to say 0.05 and 0.95, is a common regularization trick with cross-entropy, trading a small calibration bias for reduced overconfidence, and its strength is itself a hyperparameter that needs validation, not a default to copy blindly.

At production scale, cross-entropy remains the default classification loss almost everywhere, but its interaction with severe class imbalance, distribution shift, and multi-task objectives, jointly predicting slowdown at 15, 30 and 60 minutes, is an active area: weighted or focal variants reweight easy versus hard examples, and setting those weights without hand-tuning per deployment remains more art than science. On-device and quantized inference introduces its own subtlety: a model trained with full-precision cross-entropy can have its calibration measurably degraded by post-training quantization, a gap between offline training loss and deployed behavior that production teams now check for explicitly.

decision-tree.def: A model that asks yes/no questions about features and gives a constant answer in each leaf.
levels: A decision tree is a game of twenty questions. Each answer sends you down one path or another until you land on a guess.

A decision tree splits data by asking yes-or-no questions about its features, like 'is the downstream speed below 40?', and each answer sends a row down a different branch. At the end of each branch, a leaf, the tree gives one constant answer based on the training rows that ended up there. Deeper trees ask more questions and capture finer patterns, but can also memorize noise.

A tree picks, at each node, the split that most reduces impurity in the resulting two groups, for classification something like Gini impurity or the reduction in cross-entropy, for regression the reduction in squared error, searching over every feature and every possible threshold. `DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5)` limits how many questions deep the tree can go, since an unlimited tree keeps splitting until every leaf has one training row, memorizing the training set and generalizing badly. Predicting is fast: follow the questions from the root to a leaf and read off the leaf's stored value.

A single decision tree is a high-variance, low-bias model: it can represent complex, nonlinear decision boundaries and interactions between features without feature engineering, but small changes in training data can produce a very different tree, since an early split near the top changes every split below it. This instability is what ensemble methods exploit: bagging averages over many trees trained on resampled data to cancel out that variance, and boosting builds trees sequentially to correct each other's errors, and both routinely outperform a single tree by a wide margin. A tree handles categorical features and missing values gracefully and needs no feature scaling, but cannot extrapolate: a leaf's prediction is always a value seen in training, so a tree cannot predict a pattern outside anything it has seen before.

Why gradient-boosted trees dominate on tabular data like this project's, despite deep learning's dominance on images and text, is an active empirical research question: trees handle the heterogeneous, non-smooth, mixed-scale nature of tabular data, a station ID, a continuous speed, a binary weekend flag, more naturally than the smooth, gradient-friendly functions neural networks are built for. A common mistake is reading feature importance from a tree, or even a boosted ensemble, as causal: a split on downstream speed says the feature is predictive given the other features already split on, not that it causes the target, and correlated features can arbitrarily split importance between them depending on which the tree happened to pick first. Monotone constraints, forcing a prediction to only increase, never decrease, as a feature rises, are a useful way to inject known domain structure, like higher current occupancy never lowering predicted slowdown probability, that a tree would not otherwise respect on noisy data.

In production, single decision trees are essentially never deployed alone; what ships is always an ensemble, compiled to branch-free vectorized code or an on-device format like Core ML's tree ensembles for fast, low-power inference, and watched for drift by monitoring the histogram of values arriving at each split rather than retraining reflexively. An open research thread is combining trees' native strength on tabular data with representation learning from neural networks, GBT-initialized MLPs, differentiable trees, deep-forest hybrids, since neither approach alone is clearly better across the full range of real tabular datasets production teams encounter.

optimizer.def: The rule that turns gradients into parameter updates; AdamW adapts the step per parameter and adds weight decay.
levels: An optimizer is the coach that tells the model which way to nudge itself after every practice guess, so next time it guesses a little better.

The optimizer turns the gradient, which direction makes the error bigger or smaller, into an actual change to the model's numbers. Plain gradient descent just takes a step opposite the gradient; Adam is a fancier optimizer that adjusts how big a step to take for each parameter separately, based on how that parameter's gradient has behaved recently. AdamW is Adam with weight decay added, which gently shrinks the model's weights toward zero to keep them from growing too large.

Plain gradient descent updates each parameter as w ← w − η∇L, where η is the learning rate; Adam instead keeps a running average of the gradient, momentum, and of the squared gradient for every parameter, and updates using both: θ_t = θ_{t−1} − α·m̂_t/(√v̂_t + ε), where the hats denote bias-corrected averages. This gives each parameter effectively its own adaptive step size, parameters with noisy, small gradients get relatively bigger steps than under plain gradient descent. AdamW adds weight decay as a separate term subtracted directly from the weights each step, rather than folding it into the gradient the way old-style L2 regularization did, which matters for how well the regularization actually works.

Adam combines two older ideas, momentum, which smooths the gradient by averaging over recent steps so the optimizer doesn't zigzag on a noisy loss surface, and per-parameter adaptive scaling, which divides each parameter's step by the square root of its recent squared-gradient average, with bias correction terms that fix the fact that both running averages start at zero and are biased low early in training. The key insight behind AdamW, versus plain Adam with L2 regularization added to the loss, is that Adam's adaptive scaling interacts badly with L2 added inside the gradient, it gets divided by the same per-parameter scale as everything else, weakening regularization exactly where needed most, so AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient-based update entirely. Adam converges fast and is forgiving of a poorly chosen learning rate compared to plain SGD, but can generalize slightly worse than well-tuned SGD with momentum on some problems, which is why some vision models still use SGD despite Adam's convenience.

The theory behind Adam's convergence guarantees turned out to have gaps, the original paper's proof was later shown flawed for certain sequences, and AMSGrad was proposed as a fix, though in practice plain Adam or AdamW remains what almost everyone uses because the theoretical counterexamples rarely bite on real problems. A subtlety practitioners get wrong constantly: Adam's adaptive per-parameter learning rate means the effective step size for a nominal learning rate isn't comparable across models with different parameter scales, so a rate tuned for one model rarely transfers cleanly to another. Bias-correction terms matter disproportionately in the first few hundred steps and their effect washes out later, which is why warmup schedules, starting the learning rate very low and ramping up, are often paired with Adam-family optimizers specifically to avoid instability during that early, high-variance phase.

At the scale of large model training, the optimizer's memory footprint becomes a real engineering constraint: Adam and AdamW store two additional full-size buffers per parameter, roughly tripling memory needed for optimizer state beyond the model weights, which is why 8-bit Adam, factored second-moment estimates, and optimizer state sharding across devices exist specifically to make Adam-family training feasible at billions of parameters. An open research question is whether Adam-style adaptive optimizers remain necessary as scale grows, since some recent large-scale training recipes have found simpler optimizers competitive when paired with careful learning-rate schedules and normalization, suggesting some of Adam's advantage may be about forgiving hyperparameter tuning more than a fundamentally better trajectory.

fundamental-diagram.def: Flow against occupancy: rising while the road is free, falling once it is saturated. Congestion is the falling branch.
levels: Picture a hallway. A few kids can run through fast. Pack the hallway full of kids, and now nobody can move, that's the fundamental diagram, cars instead of kids.

The fundamental diagram is a plot of traffic flow, how many cars pass per minute, against how packed the road is, density or occupancy. At first, more cars means more flow, since traffic is still moving. Past a point, though, the road gets so packed that cars slow down and flow actually starts falling, that's a traffic jam.

The fundamental diagram plots flow on the vertical axis against density, or occupancy, its close proxy, on the horizontal axis: flow rises roughly linearly as density increases from empty, peaks at the road's capacity, then falls as density keeps rising and speed collapses. The falling branch, high density, low speed, low flow, is exactly what this project's slow label is trying to catch before it fully happens. Flow is approximately density times speed, so at any point on the diagram you can read off the implied average speed as the slope of a line from the origin.

The fundamental diagram assumes traffic is roughly in a steady state, a reasonable approximation over a five-minute detector interval but not instantaneously, and its exact shape, parabolic, triangular, or a more complex fitted curve, varies by road type, lane count, and weather. Its practical use in this project is diagnostic and for feature engineering, not as the model itself: since the falling branch is where flow and speed decouple from their free-flow relationship, a feature like the ratio of current speed to a station's typical high-occupancy speed carries some of the same information. The diagram breaks down at a detector level when the station itself misbehaves, a stuck loop reporting near-100 percent occupancy, or when the relationship is confounded by an incident that changes the road's actual capacity, not just its current load.

A subtlety the two-branch diagram hides: the same flow-density pair can correspond to either the free-flow branch or the congested branch, so flow and density alone are ambiguous without also knowing speed or which regime the road is in, which is why flow by itself is a weaker feature than the combination of flow, occupancy and speed together, and why practitioners who feature-engineer only on flow miss the branch information that speed makes explicit. Hysteresis is a real, well-documented deviation from the simple diagram: the flow-density relationship during the transition into congestion measurably differs from the relationship during recovery out of it, at the same density, because driver behavior differs going in versus coming out, exactly the kind of regime-dependent structure that motivates change-point models for detecting breakdown rather than a fixed threshold. Capacity itself is not a fixed number for a road segment; it drops measurably once congestion has set in, a capacity drop, part of why a jam clears more slowly than the buildup that caused it.

Production traffic systems increasingly move beyond the classical single-point fundamental diagram toward network-level and macroscopic models, cell transmission models and their learned neural analogues, that capture how a breakdown at one point propagates spatially to upstream detectors, exactly the graph-based extension this project's later lessons build toward. Open research questions include how to fuse the classical, physically grounded fundamental-diagram relationship with a purely learned model, as a prior, a feature, or a constraint on outputs, so the model respects known traffic-flow physics, flow cannot exceed capacity, speed cannot exceed free flow, rather than learning it purely from data that may not cover every regime well.

probability.def: A number between 0 and 1 saying how likely something is: 0 impossible, 1 certain, and a calibrated 0.3 should be right about three times in ten.
levels: A probability is a number that tells you how likely something is to happen, like a weather forecast saying a 30 percent chance of rain. Zero means it definitely won't happen, and one means it definitely will.

A probability is a number between 0 and 1 that measures how likely an event is; multiply by 100 to get a percent. This project's model outputs a probability, like 0.4, that traffic will be slow in 30 minutes, rather than a flat yes or no, because 0.4 and 0.95 mean very different things even though both might round to 'probably slow.' A fair coin lands heads with probability 0.5, meaning if you flipped it many times, about half would come up heads.

Formally, a probability is a number in [0, 1] assigned so the probabilities of all possible outcomes sum to 1, and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) when A and B cannot both happen. In this project, the model outputs P(slow in 30 minutes | current and recent detector readings), a conditional probability given the features it observes. `.mean()` of a column of zeros and ones computes exactly the observed share of positives, which is how the label's overall prevalence is calculated.

A probability the model outputs is only meaningful if it is calibrated: a set of rows the model calls 0.3 should, on average, actually be positive about 30 percent of the time, checked with a reliability diagram or `calibration_curve`. The model outputs a probability rather than a hard decision specifically because the decision of when to act depends on costs, a false alarm versus a missed slowdown, that are not known at training time and can change later, so deferring to a threshold chosen afterward is the right design. This assumes the training data's labels reflect the true frequency of the event under the same conditions the model will see in production, which fails when the underlying process shifts, a form of drift.

Two philosophically distinct interpretations of probability are at play here, frequentist, a long-run frequency over repeated situations, and Bayesian, a degree of belief, updatable with new evidence, and in practice a model's calibrated output is treated frequentist-style even though the model itself may be trained with Bayesian-flavored regularization, priors as weight decay. A common mistake is conflating a well-ranked model, good average precision, with a well-calibrated one, honest probabilities; a model can order rows well from most to least likely positive while its raw probability values are systematically too extreme or too conservative, exactly what post-hoc calibration, isotonic regression or Platt scaling, exists to fix. Reweighting classes to handle imbalance shifts the model's implied prior and distorts calibration in a predictable, correctable direction, an additive shift in log-odds equal to the log of the reweighting factor, which must be undone before the output can be read as a true probability again.

Production systems that act on a model's probability output treat calibration as a monitored production metric in its own right, not just a training-time diagnostic, because calibration can degrade under drift even while ranking-based metrics look stable. Research and engineering effort increasingly goes into uncertainty quantification beyond a single point probability, conformal prediction methods that give a calibrated interval with a coverage guarantee under minimal assumptions, and Bayesian or ensemble methods that separate 'the model is uncertain because the situation is inherently random' from 'the model has never seen anything like this before,' a distinction a single probability number cannot express on its own.

derivative.def: The slope of a function at one point: how fast its output changes as its input changes by a tiny amount.
levels: A derivative tells you how fast something changes, like how steep a hill is right where you are standing. If the hill is flat, the derivative is zero; if it's a steep climb, the derivative is a big number.

The derivative of a function is its slope at one exact point, showing how much the output changes if the input changes just a little. For f(x) = x², the derivative is 2x, so at x = 3 the slope is 6, the function is climbing steeply there. Derivatives are how a computer learns to improve a model, by seeing which direction makes an error go down.

The slope of a straight line is rise over run; the derivative of a curve at one point is the slope of the line that just touches the curve there, the tangent line, computed as the limit of (f(x+h) − f(x))/h as h shrinks to zero. Rules make this practical without limits: the power rule, the derivative of x^n is n·x^(n−1), the product rule, and the chain rule for functions inside functions. Example: gradient descent uses the derivative to take a step w ← w − η·(dL/dw), moving w in the direction that makes the loss L smaller.

In machine learning, the object of interest is usually a partial derivative, how the loss changes with respect to one parameter while holding the others fixed, and the gradient collects all such partial derivatives into one vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase; gradient descent moves opposite to it. The sigmoid function's own derivative has a clean closed form, σ'(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), which the chain rule uses when differentiating cross-entropy loss through a sigmoid, producing the simple result that the derivative of the loss with respect to the raw score is just predicted probability minus true label. Derivatives assume the function is smooth at the point in question; a function with a sharp corner, like the absolute-value part of a Huber loss right at its threshold, has no single well-defined derivative there, which is why such losses are defined piecewise.

Automatic differentiation, the technique behind every modern deep learning framework, computes exact derivatives of arbitrarily complex functions by applying the chain rule mechanically through a recorded computation graph, tracking, for every operation, how to pass a gradient backward through it, this is what backpropagation actually is, generalized. A subtlety practitioners often gloss over: a derivative measures local, infinitesimal behavior, and a function can have a well-behaved derivative everywhere while still being poorly conditioned for optimization, a long, narrow valley in the loss landscape, which is why gradient-based methods need momentum or adaptive scaling, as in Adam, rather than relying on the raw gradient direction alone. Numerical differentiation, approximating a derivative by evaluating f(x+h) and f(x) and dividing by h, is a useful debugging tool for checking a hand-derived or autodiff gradient, but is itself numerically unstable for very small h due to floating-point rounding, and inaccurate for large h, the classic tradeoff of finite-difference methods.

At the scale of training large models, computing and storing derivatives for every parameter is often the dominant memory cost of training, which drives techniques like gradient checkpointing, recomputing intermediate activations during the backward pass instead of storing them, trading compute for memory, and mixed-precision training, where derivatives are computed and accumulated carefully to avoid losing accuracy in low-precision arithmetic. Second-order information, derivatives of derivatives, captured in the Hessian, is what gradient-boosted trees like LightGBM actually use per split, via a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, more information than plain gradient descent uses and part of why boosted trees converge so efficiently on tabular problems; scaling that same second-order idea to neural network training at scale remains computationally expensive and an active research area.

markov.def: A Markov model assumes the future depends only on the present state; a hidden Markov model adds states you infer from noisy measurements, not observe directly.
levels: A Markov model is like a board game where the only thing that matters for your next move is which square you're standing on right now, not how you got there. A hidden Markov model is the same game played in the dark: you can't see which square you're on, only clues, and you have to guess.

In a Markov chain, the next state depends only on the current state, not on the whole history before it, weather tomorrow, in a simple toy model, might depend only on whether it's raining today, not on last week. A hidden Markov model adds a twist: the true state, like whether a road is truly free-flowing or congested, isn't directly visible, only a noisy observation of it, like measured speed, is, and the model infers the hidden state from that.

A Markov chain has states and transition probabilities, P(state at t+1 | state at t), and the Markov property is exactly the assumption that this conditional probability need not also condition on states before t. A hidden Markov model adds an emission distribution, P(observation | hidden state), for each hidden state, and an algorithm like Viterbi finds the most likely sequence of hidden states given a sequence of observations. For a traffic corridor, a hidden Markov model could model two hidden states, free flow and congested, each with its own distribution over observed speeds, and infer transitions between them from noisy speed readings alone.

The Markov property is a strong simplifying assumption, it says the current state is a sufficient statistic for predicting the future, so relevant history is already summarized in it, and much of practical modeling is really about choosing a state representation rich enough that this becomes approximately true, even when the raw process, like traffic, clearly depends on more than the current five-minute reading. This project's lag features are a workaround for exactly this: stacking several lags, speed 15, 30, 60 minutes ago, into the feature vector lets a plain classifier implicitly condition on recent history, achieving something like a higher-order Markov model without the formal machinery. Hidden Markov models fail when true dynamics are not well approximated by a small, discrete number of hidden states with stationary transition probabilities, real traffic has states that blend continuously and transition probabilities that themselves depend on time of day.

Fitting a hidden Markov model's parameters from data, typically via the Baum-Welch or EM algorithm, is a non-convex problem with many local optima, so results depend on initialization, and the number of hidden states is a modeling choice, not something the data cleanly reveals, which is why hidden Markov models are more often used as an interpretable diagnostic tool, does the data support a two-regime structure, than as the production model itself here. A subtlety: a Markov chain's stationary distribution exists and is unique only under conditions, irreducibility, aperiodicity, that traffic dynamics don't obviously satisfy, since congested at 5pm on a weekday and congested at 3am after an accident are not really the same recurring process. Practitioners sometimes reach for a hidden Markov model when what they actually want is a change-point model, detecting when the regime switched rather than continuously tracking a hidden state, a related but distinct and often simpler tool for exactly this project's breakdown-detection problem.

At production scale, explicit hidden Markov models are rarely deployed directly for traffic prediction; instead, their conceptual role, a compact hidden state summarizing history, updated as new observations arrive, is absorbed into recurrent and state-space neural models, a GRU is, informally, a learned, nonlinear generalization of a hidden Markov model's state update, without the constraint of discrete states or a fixed transition matrix. Research interest persists in reinforcement learning, as partially observable Markov decision processes, and in interpretable regime-detection systems where a small number of discrete, human-nameable states, free flow, congested, recovering, is itself a product requirement, which pulls some production systems back toward classical hidden-Markov-like structure specifically for that interpretability.

boosting.def: Bagging averages independent models on resampled data; boosting builds models sequentially to fix earlier mistakes; an ensemble is any such combination.
levels: Boosting is playing many tiny question-games in a row, where each new game only tries to fix what the games before it got wrong, and all the little answers get added up at the end. Bagging is like asking a hundred different friends to each guess separately, then averaging all their guesses together. An ensemble is just the word for a team of guessers working together instead of one guesser alone.

An ensemble is any model made of several smaller models combined. Bagging trains many trees independently, each on a random resample of the training rows, and averages their predictions, canceling out each tree's individual mistakes, this is what a random forest does. Boosting instead trains trees one after another, where each new tree fixes the errors the trees before it made, summing their outputs rather than averaging, with LightGBM in this course being a boosting method.

In bagging, each of B trees trains on a bootstrap sample, rows drawn with replacement, and the final prediction averages all B trees' outputs, reducing variance because their individual errors are only weakly correlated. In boosting, the model starts with a constant prediction F₀ and repeatedly adds a small tree h_m fitted to the current residual errors, scaled by a learning rate η: F_m = F_{m−1} + η·h_m, so each new tree corrects what the sum so far still gets wrong. `lgb.train(params, ...)` in this project runs gradient boosting; `bagging_fraction=0.8` adds a bagging-style random row subsample inside that boosting process too, since the two ideas combine.

Bagging primarily reduces variance: since each bootstrap-trained tree is a noisy, high-variance estimator, averaging many roughly-independent noisy estimators shrinks the noise without changing the average bias, which is why deep, low-bias, high-variance trees, not shallow ones, are the right base learner for bagging. Boosting instead primarily reduces bias: it starts with a deliberately weak model and iteratively adds capacity exactly where the current model is wrong, which can reduce both bias and, with the right learning rate and enough regularization, keep variance in check too, but boosting is more prone to overfitting than bagging if run too long without early stopping. Both are ensembles in the general sense, but for different statistical reasons, which is why their failure modes differ: bagging fails gracefully, adding more trees rarely hurts, while boosting can actively get worse past its optimal number of rounds, exactly why validation-based early stopping is essential.

Friedman's framing of boosting as gradient descent in function space clarifies what generalizes: each added tree approximates the negative gradient of the loss with respect to current predictions, so the choice of loss, squared error, absolute error, Huber, logistic, determines what each tree is actually fitting, and modern implementations go further, using the loss's second-order Hessian information too, why a leaf's optimal value has the closed form −Σg/(Σh + λ) rather than a plain average of residuals. A common mistake is treating `feature_fraction` and `bagging_fraction` in a boosting library as afterthoughts rather than what they are: injecting bagging-style randomness into a boosting procedure specifically to fight the overfitting pure boosting is prone to, a hybrid most production boosting libraries use by default. The persistent empirical finding across many tabular benchmarks is that boosted tree ensembles beat both single trees and, at this data size and type, often beat deep neural networks, which motivates this project's use of LightGBM even as later lessons introduce neural and graph models.

In production, boosted ensembles are typically compiled to branch-free, vectorized or hardware-specific code, or shipped on-device through frameworks like Core ML's tree ensemble support, quantized for latency, and monitored for drift via the histogram of values reaching each split rather than the raw input features directly, since that histogram is a cheap, always-available signature of what the model is actually doing at inference time. Active research threads include margin-based generalization theory for boosting, hybrids combining boosted trees with learned neural representations, GBT-initialized MLPs, deep forests, and uncertainty quantification for tree ensembles, natural-gradient boosting, quantile boosting, or wrapping conformal prediction around an otherwise point-valued boosted model.

batch-normalization.def: A layer that rescales its inputs to have roughly zero mean and unit variance across each mini-batch, with a learned scale and shift, so training is faster and more forgiving.
levels: Batch normalization is like a teacher making sure everyone in the class is standing at about the same height before a group photo, so nobody's tiny voice or giant shout throws off the whole picture.

When training a neural network, the numbers flowing through each layer can grow too large or shrink too small as training goes on, which makes learning slow or unstable. Batch normalization fixes this by rescaling each layer's inputs, for every mini-batch of training examples, so they have roughly zero average and a standard spread, then lets the network learn its own small adjustment, a scale and a shift, on top of that if it needs one.

For a mini-batch of activations x, batch normalization computes y = γ·(x − μ_B)/√(σ_B² + ε) + β, where μ_B and σ_B² are the batch's mean and variance, ε is a tiny constant avoiding division by zero, and γ and β are learned parameters the network can use to undo the normalization if that helps. It's typically inserted between a layer's linear transformation and its nonlinearity, like a ReLU. At test time, since there's no batch to compute statistics from a single example, a running average of μ_B and σ_B² collected during training is used instead.

Batch normalization's practical benefit, faster, more stable training that tolerates a higher learning rate and is less sensitive to initialization, is well established empirically, though the original explanation, reducing internal covariate shift, has been challenged; later work argued its main effect is smoothing the loss landscape, making gradients more predictable step to step, a different and more defensible theoretical story. A key assumption is a large-enough, representative mini-batch: with very small batches, batch statistics become noisy estimates of the true population statistics, which can hurt rather than help, motivating alternatives like layer normalization that don't depend on batch size at all. It interacts subtly with other regularization: because batch statistics add a form of noise, each example's normalized value depends on which other examples share its batch, batch normalization has a mild regularizing effect similar to, and sometimes redundant with, dropout.

The train and test discrepancy, computing statistics from the current batch during training but using a fixed running average at test time, is a genuine source of bugs when the deployment distribution differs from training, since the running average no longer reflects what the model is actually seeing, one reason batch normalization can silently degrade under real-world drift in a way easy to miss if only training-time metrics are checked. Practitioners commonly get bitten by its interaction with distributed training: statistics computed only within one device's local mini-batch, rather than synchronized across devices, can differ meaningfully from the intended global-batch statistics at large batch sizes, which is why sync batch norm exists specifically for multi-GPU training. Modern architectures, transformers especially, largely moved to layer normalization or RMSNorm instead, partly because sequence models often have variable-length, small-batch settings where batch statistics are unreliable, so treating batch normalization as universally the normalization choice, rather than one architecture-specific tool among several, is a dated assumption.

On-device and low-latency inference settings fold batch normalization's learned scale and shift directly into the preceding linear layer's weights at deployment time, since at inference the running statistics are fixed constants, a standard batch-norm-folding optimization that removes the normalization as a separate runtime operation entirely with no change in output. Research continues on normalization schemes that combine the training benefits of batch normalization with robustness to small or variable batch sizes and to distribution shift at inference, since production traffic-prediction and other streaming systems often score one example, or a handful, at a time, exactly the regime where the classical batch-statistics assumption is weakest.
